Now I have enough material from multiple sources. Let me compile the verse-by-verse notes.

# Nehemiah 11 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview of the Chapter

**David Guzik (Enduring Word)** summarises: After the walls were rebuilt and spiritual renewal had taken place, Nehemiah turned to repopulating Jerusalem. The city needed more people for prosperity, defence, and strength. Leaders set the example by living there; a lottery brought one in ten; volunteers received a special blessing. The bulk of the chapter is a detailed roster of families, priests, Levites, gatekeepers, and officials who settled in Jerusalem and throughout Judah. [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-11/]

**Precept Austin** notes that Nehemiah 11–12 can prompt the question, "Why did God put this in His inspired Word?" Citing Derek Kidner: "It is not bureaucratic pedantry that has preserved these names. The point is, once more, that these people and their chronicler are conscious of their roots and of their structure as God's company. This is no rabble of refugees … they have the dignity of order and of known relationships." [preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-11-commentary]

---

## v. 1 — The Leaders Settle; a Tithe by Lot

**Traditional Reading (multiple sources):**

- **The leaders dwelt at Jerusalem.** Gill says this was proper — Jerusalem was the metropolis, and their office obliged them to dwell there for governance, protection, and to set an example. [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/nehemiah-11.html]
- **The rest cast lots to bring one out of ten.** Gill explains that people were reluctant to settle in Jerusalem: it was the target of enemy rage, and country living was more profitable. The lot was used to oblige settlement so the city could be rebuilt, repopulated, and defended. [same source]
- **JFB** adds that Jerusalem was a dangerous posting because enemies were plotting against it, so "residence in it at such a juncture was attended with expense and various annoyances from which a country life was entirely free." [biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/nehemiah/11.htm]
- **Pulpit Commentary** says Nehemiah had to look lower than the nobles (already resident; see 2:16) to obtain new settlers from the ranks of the "people." The Jews used the lot believing "the whole disposing thereof was of the Lord" (Prov 16:33). Ewald supposed the one-in-ten was meant as a permanent proportion, but Pulpit says the narrative implies rather a one-time addition of a tenth of the country population. [biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/nehemiah/11.htm]
- **Bob Utley** (cited by Precept Austin): Since the siege of 586 BC, no one wanted to live in the city. The leaders (wealthy laymen) and temple personnel were the only large groups within the walls (cf. 11:3; 2:16–17). The casting of lots "had religious connotations … It was a way to know the will of YHWH." [preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-11-commentary]
- **"The holy city"** — This is the first time Jerusalem is so named in Nehemiah. It is called holy because of the temple and the worship of God there (Gill), and because it was the place where YHWH dwelt (Isa 48:2; 52:1; Dan 9:24, cited by Utley). [preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-11-commentary] [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/nehemiah-11.html]

---

## v. 2 — Volunteers Are Blessed

**Traditional Reading:**

- **Cambridge Bible** distinguishes three classes of dwellers here: (a) the princes (rulers), (b) the ten percent chosen by lot and forcibly transferred, and (c) those who voluntarily migrated. The volunteers are not to be confused with those chosen by lot — they went of their own accord, moved by public spirit. The people's blessing "shows the enthusiasm aroused by their patriotic action; at the same time, it may denote that residence in Jerusalem was recognised to be fraught with danger." [biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/nehemiah/11.htm]
- **Gill**: They were "not taken by lot, but of their own accord settled at Jerusalem; they praised them for it, and wished them all happiness and prosperity, since they denied themselves of ease and profit for the sake of the public good." Gill notes that this distinguishes the list here from 1 Chronicles 9 — that list includes all settlers, whether voluntary or by lot; this one only those fixed by lot. [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/nehemiah-11.html]
- **Poole** adds: "Because they denied themselves, and their own safety and profit, for the public good; for this city was the butt of all the malicious plots of their enemies; and for the present it was rather chargeable than beneficial to its inhabitants." [biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/nehemiah/11.htm]
- **David Guzik** draws out the cost: Volunteers gave up land, social ties, and comfort; they lived knowing they were a target; they had "a unique pioneer spirit" and "the ability to endure some measure of hardship or discomfort to accomplish a greater work for God's kingdom." He connects it to Zechariah 4:10 — "who has despised the day of small things?" — and to the future New Jerusalem (Rev 21:2). [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-11/]

**Application (Precept Austin / Steven Cole):** Ministry involves a willingness to live where God wants you to live. These people "had to pull up roots where they were already established, give up their acreage in the country." Christians should ask, "Where does God want me to live?" — determined in large measure by ministry potential. [preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-11-commentary]

---

## v. 3 — Heads of the Provinces; Everyone Else in Their Own Towns

**Traditional Reading:**

- **Gill**: "These are the chief of the province" — i.e., of Judea, reduced to a province by Babylon and now under Persia. Everyone else dwelt "in his possession in their cities" — the properties their ancestors had held. "Israel" here means the general populace of Judah and Benjamin plus members of other tribes who returned with them, along with priests, Levites, Nethinim, and Solomon's servants. [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/nehemiah-11.html]
- **Pulpit Commentary**: Those who removed from the country to Jerusalem "quitted their 'possessions,' often, it may be, exchanging riches for poverty, a comfortable house for one half in ruins (Neh 7:4), and the life of a small landed proprietor for that of an artisan or hired labourer." Hence the blessings on volunteers. [biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/nehemiah/11.htm]
- **Poole**: "Israel" here means the generality of the people, whether of Judah, Benjamin, or any other tribe. He calls them Israel rather than Judah "partly because there were many of the other tribes now joined and incorporated with them." [biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/nehemiah/11.htm]

---

## vv. 4–6 — Descendants of Judah in Jerusalem

**Traditional Reading:**

- **Pulpit Commentary**: Athaiah (called Uthai in 1 Chron 9:4) is listed with a genealogy that differs from Chronicles — "Both lists are of course abbreviations of a far longer one, and it has happened that the two writers have in no case selected for mention the same name." [biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/nehemiah/11.htm]
- **Poole**: Athaiah represents "his family and relations with him, and under him as their head." [biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/nehemiah/11.htm]
- v. 5: **Pulpit** notes Maaseiah is called "Asaiah" in 1 Chronicles and designated as "the Shilonite," i.e., a descendant of Shelah, youngest son of Judah. The word *ben* ("son") before "Shiloni" is likely a copyist's error — it should read "the Shilonite," not "son of Shiloni." [biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/nehemiah/11.htm]
- v. 6: The descendants of Perez totalled **468 valiant men** — "fighting men, men able to bear arms and serve in the wars" (Pulpit). Poole adds this was especially proper "because of its many enemies round about it." [biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/nehemiah/11.htm] [biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/nehemiah/11.htm]

---

## vv. 7–9 — Descendants of Benjamin in Jerusalem

**Traditional Reading:**

- **Pulpit Commentary**: Notes that a verse equivalent to 1 Chronicles 9:6 seems to have fallen out — the descendants of Zerah (who formed more than half the Jewish element and 690 fighting men) are missing. Sallu's genealogy here uses different ancestor names than Chronicles — "the two writers singling out for mention different ancestors." [biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/nehemiah/11.htm]
- v. 8: Gabbai and Sallai are not mentioned in Chronicles. The number 928 here vs 956 in 1 Chronicles 9:9 — "Probably in one place or the other the figures have suffered corruption" (Pulpit). **Poole** notes there were more from Benjamin than Judah "because the city did chiefly and most properly belong to that tribe." [biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/nehemiah/11.htm] [biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/nehemiah/11.htm]
- v. 9: **Joel son of Zichri** was "their overseer" — the commandant of the city under Nehemiah (Pulpit, citing 2 Kings 25:19 where *pakid* has this sense). **Judah son of Hassenuah** was "over the Second District" — "second over the city," next in authority to Joel. [biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/nehemiah/11.htm]
- **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary**: Jerusalem was originally in Benjamin's allotment, "which may account for the larger number of Benjamites already living there." [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/nehemiah-11.html]

---

## vv. 10–14 — The Priests in Jerusalem

**Traditional Reading:**

- v. 10: **Pulpit Commentary** says the word *ben* ("son") has accidentally crept in again — it should read "Jedaiah, Joiarib, Jachin" as family names, not personal genealogies (compare 1 Chron 9:10). Jedaiah and Joiarib were two of the chief priestly families; Jachin was descended from the head of the 21st course in David's time. [biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/nehemiah/11.htm]
- v. 11: **Seraiah** (called Azariah in 1 Chron 9:11) designates the high priestly family of the time. He was grandson, not son, of Hilkiah (Ezra 7:1). "Ruler of the house of God" means the family that furnished the high priests — the actual high priest was Eliashib (Neh 12:10; 13:4). [biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/nehemiah/11.htm]
- **Poole**: Seraiah was "one of the chief priests; who ruled with and under the high priest" (citing Num 3:32; 1 Chron 9:11; 2 Chron 19:11). [biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/nehemiah/11.htm]
- vv. 12–14: Three groups of priests are listed: 822 who "did the work of the house" (ordinary priests in courses), 242 "leaders of families," and 128 "mighty men of valour." **Pulpit** says "mighty men of valour" here means not courage in battle but "very able men for the work of the service of the house of God" (as 1 Chron 9:13). The total is 1,192 priests. **Zabdiel** is "son of Haggedolim" (margin), not "son of one of the great men." [biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/nehemiah/11.htm]

---

## vv. 15–18 — The Levites in Jerusalem

**Traditional Reading:**

- vv. 15–16: **Shemaiah** was a descendant of Merari (1 Chron 9:14). Together with **Shabbethai and Jozabad**, he supervised "the outward business of the house of God." Pulpit explains: "its worldly affairs and money matters" — like the appointment of deacons "to serve tables" in Acts 6:2–5. Poole says this covered "things belonging to the temple and its service, which were to be done without it, or abroad in the country, as for the gathering in of the voluntary contributions, or other necessary provisions." [biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/nehemiah/11.htm] [biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/nehemiah/11.htm]
- v. 17: **Mattaniah** (descendant of Asaph) "was the principal to begin the thanksgiving in prayer" — i.e., the leader of the choir or precentor. Bakbukiah was second; Abda (Obadiah in 1 Chron 9:16) held the third place. Poole notes this refers to "the public and solemn prayers and praises which were constantly joined with the morning and evening sacrifice." [biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/nehemiah/11.htm] [biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/nehemiah/11.htm]
- v. 18: **284 Levites** in the holy city. **Pulpit** observes the small proportion of Levites to priests (less than one-third), "which has been already noticed (see comment on Ezra 8:15)." [biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/nehemiah/11.htm]

---

## v. 19 — The Gatekeepers

**Traditional Reading:**

- **Akkub and Talmon** are familiar names (see Ezra 2:42). They and their associates numbered **172 men**. In 1 Chronicles 9:22 the number is 212 — Pulpit notes the discrepancy without resolving it. [biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/nehemiah/11.htm]

---

## vv. 20–21 — The Rest of Israel; the Temple Servants on Ophel

**Traditional Reading:**

- v. 20: The rest of the Israelites, priests, and Levites lived in the villages of Judah, "each on his own inheritance" — in the cities, houses, and estates their ancestors had held (Gill). [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/nehemiah-11.html]
- v. 21: **The temple servants (Nethinim) lived on Ophel** — the southern prolongation of the temple hill, "a sort of suburb of Jerusalem, sometimes reckoned as part of the city, sometimes as distinct from it." It was convenient for the Nethinim, who performed menial temple offices. **Ziha** represents the leading Nethinim family (Ezra 2:43; Neh 7:46). [biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/nehemiah/11.htm]

---

## vv. 22–24 — Overseers, Singers, and the King's Agent

**Traditional Reading:**

- v. 22: **Uzzi son of Bani**, a descendant of Asaph, was "overseer of the Levites in Jerusalem … over the business of the house of God." As Shabbethai and Jozabad handled outward business (v. 16), Uzzi supervised internal business. He appears again at the wall dedication (Neh 12:42). [biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/nehemiah/11.htm]
- **Poole** adds that the singers' role in this oversight was fitting: they were Levites (to whose care such things belonged), they resided constantly in Jerusalem (unlike other Levites who served by turns), and their singing duties left them with more leisure for administration. [biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/nehemiah/11.htm]
- v. 23: **"A command from the king concerning the singers."** Pulpit says Artaxerxes had assigned a stipend from the royal revenue for the support of Levite singers, paid daily. Two possible reasons: (1) the singing Levites were regarded as those who prayed "for the life of the king and of his sons" (Ezra 6:10); (2) they were so few (128) they had to be constantly on duty. [biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/nehemiah/11.htm]
- **Poole** offers three interpretations of "the king's command": (1) David's original constitution; (2) the Persian king's decree at Ezra/Nehemiah's request; or (3) Nehemiah's own command, called "the king's" because done by the king's deputy with royal authority (as with Ezra in Ezra 7:18, 20, 23). [biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/nehemiah/11.htm]
- v. 24: **Pethahiah son of Meshezabel**, of the descendants of Zerah (son of Judah), was "the king's agent in every matter concerning the people." Pulpit notes his mention reveals the earlier catalogue was incomplete — no descendants of Zerah had been listed among Jerusalem's dwellers (all were sons of Perez in v. 6). His exact office is undetermined: perhaps he received and forwarded petitions and complaints as intermediary between the Persian king and the Jewish people. [biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/nehemiah/11.htm]
- **Poole** suggests he was "chief justiciary under Nehemiah," determining civil causes by Persian law, or handling matters of tribute and grievances. [biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/nehemiah/11.htm]

---

## vv. 25–30 — Towns of Judah

**Traditional Reading:**

- **Pulpit Commentary** provides detailed identifications: **Kirjath-arba** is Hebron (the old name had reasserted itself during the exile); **Dibon** is not the Moabite town but ancient Dimonah (Josh 15:21–26); **Jekabzeel** is Kabzeel (Josh 15:21); **Jeshua** is mentioned only here; **Moladah** and **Beth-pelet** appear in Joshua 15; **Hazar-shual** means "village of foxes"; **Ziklag** was David's city given by Achish (1 Sam 27:6); **Mekonah** is unique to this verse; **En-rimmon** is the combined "Ain and Rimmon" of Josh 15:32; **Zareah** (Zoreah) and **Jarmuth** were in the Shephelah; **Zanoah** and **Adullam** (David's cave) were near Jarmuth; **Lachish** was Sennacherib's target; **Azekah** was fortified by Rehoboam. [biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/nehemiah/11.htm]
- v. 30: "**From Beersheba to the Valley of Hinnom**" — the southernmost to the northernmost parts of Judah. [biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/nehemiah/11.htm]
- **Dr. Constable**: These were towns south of Jerusalem, in the territory of Judah. Nehemiah mentions 17 prominent towns in Judah (vv. 25–30). [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/nehemiah-11.html]

---

## vv. 31–35 — Towns of Benjamin

**Traditional Reading:**

- **Pulpit**: The Benjamites dwelt "from Geba to Michmash, and Aija, and Bethel" — all near each other (Isa 10:28–29). **Anathoth** was a Levitical city (Josh 21:18), on the road from Geba to Jerusalem (Isa 10:30). **Nob** was still nearer the capital, visible from it (Isa 10:32), infamous for Doeg's massacre of the priests (1 Sam 22:18–19). **Ananiah** is mentioned only here. **Hazor** as a Benjamite city appears only here. **Ramah** (modern er-Ram) is the famous town just north of Jerusalem. **Gittaim** is a Benjamite town from 2 Sam 4:3. **Hadid** (modern Haditheh) is three miles east of Ludd. **Zeboim** is not otherwise known as a town, but a "valley of Zeboim" appears in 1 Sam 13:18. **Neballat** appears only here. **Lod** (Lydda in Acts) was at the eastern edge of the maritime plain; **Ono** is joined with Lod in 1 Chron 8:12 and Ezra 2:33. The "**Valley of the Craftsmen**" (*Ge-haharasim*) — its origin is unknown. [biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/nehemiah/11.htm]
- **Constable**: These were towns north of Jerusalem stretching toward Samaria — 15 towns of Benjamin. Together with Judah's 17 towns, these were the two sections of the Persian province of Yehud (Judah). [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/nehemiah-11.html]

---

## v. 36 — Levite Divisions in Judah and Benjamin

**Traditional Reading:**

- **Pulpit**: "The exact sense is obscure, but we may gather from the passage that a certain number of Levites were dispersed among the Benjamite cities. They were not now numerous enough to have any cities to themselves." [biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/nehemiah/11.htm]
- **Poole**: "For the Levites (those of them who were not settled in Jerusalem) there were divisions, i.e. places appointed for them, and distributed among them." [biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/nehemiah/11.htm]
- **Constable**: "The Levites lived among the general population, as when the Israelites first entered the land." [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/nehemiah-11.html]

---

## Protestant Traditions: Points of Emphasis

While no major doctrinal divide exists on Nehemiah 11 (it is a largely genealogical/administrative chapter), different traditions draw out distinct applications:

- **Reformed / Presbyterian (Poole, Gill, JFB):** Emphasise God's sovereignty in the lot ("the whole disposing thereof was of the Lord," Prov 16:33) and the ordering of the civil and religious community under God's providence. Poole notes the rulers' obligation by office and the people's willing self-denial for the public good — themes of covenant duty. [biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/nehemiah/11.htm] [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/nehemiah-11.html]

- **Baptist (Garner-Howes, Gill):** Stress the volunteers' special blessing — a free-church emphasis on willing, personal commitment over compulsion: "Volunteers in the Lord's work receive the special blessing." [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/nehemiah-11.html]

- **Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik):** Highlights the "pioneer spirit," the cost of following God to uncomfortable places, and typological connections to the New Jerusalem (Rev 21:2). Application is personal and devotional — willingness to "despise not the day of small things." [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-11/]

- **Evangelical emphasis on "every-member ministry" (Precept Austin / Steven Cole):** Uses the chapter to argue that all believers, not just clergy, are in ministry. Long lists of obscure names show that "faithfulness, not fame, is the issue" and that "God notices even if others do not." Every role — priest, gatekeeper, farmer, singer — was vital. [preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-11-commentary]

---

## Other Views

**Modern Scholarship:**

- **NET Bible notes** could not be fetched within limits, but the search results did not surface major critical disputes over this chapter. The chapter is generally seen as an administrative supplement to Nehemiah 7, listing the repopulation of Persian Yehud. Constable's notes reflect this mainstream scholarly approach — identifying the two sections of the Persian province. [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/nehemiah-11.html]
- **Light of Israel Bible Commentary** notes that Nehemiah's plan of "tithing the people" showed "some genius but it surely worked a great hardship on many settlers who were not especially qualified or gifted for city living." [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/loi/nehemiah-11.html]

**Catholic and Orthodox readings:** Searches on newadvent.org, catholic.com, and oca.org did not return specific verse-by-verse treatments of Nehemiah 11 within the search limits. These traditions generally follow the same historical-grammatical reading on such a genealogical chapter, with perhaps greater typological interest in Jerusalem as "the holy city" prefiguring the Church.

---

*Sources consulted: Enduring Word (Guzik), Precept Austin, Pulpit Commentary, Matthew Poole, John Gill (via StudyLight), Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (via Bible Hub), Cambridge Bible for Schools and Colleges (via Bible Hub), Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary (via StudyLight), Dr. Constable's Expository Notes (via StudyLight), Light of Israel Bible Commentary (via StudyLight), Gray's Concise Bible Commentary (via StudyLight).*
